entry: Australian children's music group formed in [[Sydney]], New South Wales, in 1991, drawing on concepts of [[Early childhood education|early childhood education]]. Its act features costumed characters such as Dorothy the Dinosaur. Its albums, DVDs and programs have been produced independently since its inception. Popularity peaked after the group broke into the American market in the early 2000s. It was ranked at the top of *Business Review Weekly*'s list of top-earning Australian entertainers four years in a row. The group has sold 23 million DVDs and 7 million CDs and was inducted into the ARIA Hall of Fame.

American crime drama television series broadcast on [[HBO]] from June 2, 2002, to March 9, 2008. Created by David Simon, a former police reporter, and set in [[Baltimore]], it ran 60 episodes over five seasons. Each season examined a different institution: the illegal drug trade, the port system, city government, education and schools, and the print news media. Critics lauded its scripting and an uncommonly accurate exploration of society, politics and urban life, but the series received average ratings and won no major television awards during its original broadcast. It later developed a cult following.

1939 American musical fantasy film produced by [[Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer]] and based on [[The Wonderful Wizard of Oz|L. Frank Baum's 1900 novel]]. Victor Fleming primarily directed it before leaving to take over the troubled *Gone with the Wind*. The film stars [[Judy Garland]] as Dorothy Gale and is celebrated for its three-strip Technicolor. It received five nominations for [[Academy Awards]] and won for Best Original Song, "Over the Rainbow," and Best Original Score. It did not make a profit until its 1949 re-release. A 1956 television broadcast on [[CBS]] reintroduced it to the public. According to the U.S. [[Library of Congress]], it is the most seen film in cinematic history. It was selected for the National Film Registry in 1989, and it is one of the few films on [[UNESCO]]'s Memory of the World register.

1900 children's fantasy novel by L. Frank Baum and the first book in the Oz series. A Kansas farm girl is carried by a [[Tornado|cyclone]] to the Land of Oz, where she learns she must destroy the Wicked Witch of the West to return home. It was first published by the George M. Hill Company in 1900 and had sold 3 million copies by the time it entered the public domain in 1956. Its success and a 1902 Broadway musical led Baum to write 13 additional Oz books. The [[Library of Congress]] has called it "America's greatest and best-loved homegrown fairytale."

American science fiction drama television series created by Chris Carter. It aired on Fox from 1993 to 2002, with later revivals in 2016 and 2018. It follows [[Federal Bureau of Investigation|FBI]] special agents Fox Mulder, a believer in the [[Paranormal|paranormal]], and Dana Scully, a skeptic, who investigate unsolved cases known as the "X-Files." Its long-term story arc drew criticism, yet it became a pop culture touchstone that tapped into public mistrust of governments. By its conclusion it was the longest-running science fiction series in American television history.

Family of [[Flowering plant|flowering plants]] known as the [[Tea|tea]] family, comprising shrubs and trees, including the economically important tea plant and the ornamental [[Camellia|camellias]]. It has from seven to 40 [[Genus|genera]], depending on the source and the method of circumscription used. Its leaves are simple, alternate, serrated and usually glossy, and most genera are evergreen, although *Stewartia* and *Franklinia* are deciduous. The flowers are usually pink or white, large and showy, and often strongly scented. Members have multiple stamens and distinctive pseudopollen. Most but not all species are native to China and East Asia, and the family is also found in Southeast Asia, tropical South America and the southeastern United States. The leaves of [[Camellia sinensis]] are used to produce tea, the family's best-known economic product.

[[Ancient Greece|Ancient Greek]] theatrical culture that flourished from 700 BC. At its centre was [[Athens]], where theatre was institutionalized as part of the Dionysia festival honoring the god [[Dionysus]]. [[Tragedy|Tragedy]], comedy and the satyr play emerged there as the three dramatic genres; tragedy is dated to the late 500 BC and comedy to 490 BC. The festival was possibly organized to foster loyalty among the tribes of Attica, and it was created around 508 BC. Athens exported the festival to its numerous colonies. Modern Western theatre borrows from this tradition its technical terminology, genre classification, and many of its themes, stock characters and plot elements.

Ancient Egyptian city on the [[Nile]] about 800 km south of the [[Mediterranean Sea|Mediterranean]], whose ruins lie within modern [[Luxor]]. Known to the Egyptians as Waset, it was the main city of the fourth Upper Egyptian nome and the capital of [[Egypt]] for long periods during the Middle Kingdom and New Kingdom. From the end of the New Kingdom it was called the "City of [[Amun]]", chief of the Theban Triad of deities. It was a religious center and the most venerated city in many periods of Egyptian history. The site includes the temples of Karnak and Luxor on the eastern bank of the Nile and a necropolis of large royal and private cemeteries on the western bank. In 1979 UNESCO classified the ruins as a [[World Heritage Site]].

Hypothetical planet in the early [[Solar System]] that, according to the [[Giant-impact hypothesis|giant-impact hypothesis]], collided with the proto-Earth around 4.50 billion years ago. Some of the ejected debris re-coalesced to form the [[Moon]]. Theia is thought to have been about the size of [[Mars]] and to have formed at the L4 or L5 [[Lagrange point|Lagrange points]] of Earth's orbit. Its name parallels that of the Titan Theia in [[Greek mythology]], mother of the Moon goddess Selene. Lunar rocks have isotope ratios nearly identical to Earth's, and Theia's composition remains disputed.

Belief in [[God]] or gods. In its narrow sense, theism refers to belief in a single creator deity who is all-powerful, all-knowing and all-benevolent. Types are distinguished by the number of gods affirmed: [[Monotheism|monotheism]] accepts one god and polytheism several. Other classifications focus on the relation between God and the world. Classical theism holds that God is distinct from the world yet can engage with it, while [[Deism|deism]] holds that the world operates by its own laws without divine intervention and [[Pantheism|pantheism]] identifies God with the world. Theism is contrasted with [[Atheism|atheism]] and agnosticism. Although it is not itself a religion, theism is central to the [[Abrahamic religions]] and to [[Hinduism]], Sikhism and other faiths. Arguments for theism include ontological, cosmological and teleological arguments, while arguments from evil maintain that the presence of evil undermines the claim that God exists.

[[Athens|Athenian]] politician and general of non-aristocratic background who championed sea power. Elected archon in 493 BC, he persuaded the Athenians in 483 BC to build a fleet of 200 triremes, which proved crucial in the coming conflict with Persia. He commanded the Athenian navy at the battles of Artemisium and Salamis in 480 BC, where his subterfuge lured the Persian fleet into the straits and the decisive Greek victory turned the war. He was ostracized in 472 or 471 BC and went into exile in Argos. Spartans then implicated him in an alleged treasonous plot, and he fled to Persia, where King Artaxerxes I made him governor of Magnesia. [[Plutarch]] called him "the man most instrumental in achieving the salvation of Greece."

Bitter [[Alkaloid|alkaloid]] that is the principal alkaloid of *Theobroma cacao*, the cacao plant, and is found in [[Chocolate|chocolate]], [[Tea|tea]] and other foods. It is used in industry as an additive and as a precursor to some [[Cosmetics|cosmetics]]. Theobromine is a metabolite of [[Caffeine|caffeine]] that is processed in the [[Liver|liver]] and peaks in the blood 2–3 hours after ingestion. It acts mainly by inhibiting adenosine receptors and is a mild heart stimulant and bronchodilator in humans. Because [[Dog|dogs]] and [[Cat|cats]] metabolize it slowly, it can be toxic or fatal to them.

Form of government in which one or more deities are recognized as supreme ruling authorities, giving divine guidance to human intermediaries who hold executive, legislative or judicial power. The term, from the Ancient Greek for "rule of God," was coined by [[Josephus|Flavius Josephus]] in the first century AD to describe the government of the [[Jews]] in the kingdoms of [[Ancient Israel and Judah|Israel and Judah]]. The [[Holy See]] is a current example: after the [[Papal States]] were annexed by the [[Kingdom of Italy]] in 1870, the Lateran Treaty of 1929 created [[Vatican City]], where the [[Pope|pope]] is elected for life by the College of Cardinals. Hybrid systems include Iran, where a Supreme Leader with clerical credentials oversees an Islamic republic enforcing Sharia-derived legislation, and Saudi Arabia, an absolute monarchy whose religious councils shape policy.

Precision optical instrument for measuring [[Angle|angles]] between visible points in the horizontal and vertical planes. Its traditional use is land [[Surveying|surveying]], but it is also used in building and infrastructure construction, and in specialized fields such as [[Meteorology|meteorology]] and [[Rocket|rocket]] launching. A movable [[Telescope|telescope]] rotates around horizontal and vertical axes and provides angular readouts, which can be accurate to microradians or seconds of arc. Angles from a single position can be used to draw a plan or to position objects according to an existing plan. The modern theodolite has evolved into the total station, which measures angles and distances electronically and records them directly to computer memory.

Hungarian Jewish journalist and lawyer who was the father of modern political [[Zionism]]. After a brief legal career in [[Vienna]], he became Paris correspondent for the Viennese newspaper *Neue Freie Presse*. Confronted with [[Antisemitism|antisemitism]] in Vienna, he concluded that Jewish assimilation was impossible and that Jews required a Jewish state. He published *Der Judenstaat* in 1896. In 1897 he convened the First Zionist Congress in [[Basel]], Switzerland, and was elected president of the Zionist Organization. He appealed unsuccessfully to German emperor Wilhelm II and to [[Abdul Hamid II|Ottoman sultan Abdul Hamid II]] for support. At the Sixth Zionist Congress in 1903 he presented the Uganda Scheme, a proposed temporary refuge in British East Africa, which was rejected. His remains were taken to Israel and reinterred on Mount Herzl in 1949.

German classical scholar, historian, jurist and politician whose work on Roman law had a significant impact on the German civil code. He received the 1902 Nobel Prize in Literature for his historical writings, including *The History of Rome*. He held professorships in law at Leipzig, Zurich and Breslau before teaching Roman history at the University of Berlin from 1861. He helped create and manage the German Archaeological Institute in Rome and served as chief editor of the *Corpus Inscriptionum Latinarum*, a collection of Latin inscriptions that provided an empirical foundation for studying Roman administration. He sat in the Prussian and German parliaments as a liberal nationalist, initially criticizing [[Otto von Bismarck|Otto von Bismarck]] before supporting German unification under Prussian leadership.

German philosopher, cultural theorist and music critic who was a leading member of the Frankfurt School of critical theory. As a critic of [[Fascism|fascism]] and of what he called the culture industry, he wrote *Dialectic of Enlightenment* (1947), *Minima Moralia* (1951) and *Negative Dialectics* (1966), which strongly influenced the European New Left. A classically trained musician, he studied composition with Alban Berg, and he collaborated with [[Thomas Mann]] on Mann's novel *Doctor Faustus* (1947) while both lived in California as exiles during the Second World War. After returning to Frankfurt he debated [[Karl Popper]] on the limitations of positivist science and criticized [[Martin Heidegger]]'s language of authenticity. His posthumously published *Aesthetic Theory* (1970) was planned for dedication to [[Samuel Beckett]].

Eastern Roman empress from 527 and wife of Emperor [[Justinian I]]. Born to a bear-keeper in [[Constantinople]], she worked as an actress and courtesan in her youth before marrying Justinian. She was one of his chief political advisers and played a crucial role in suppressing the Nika riots of 532. She and Justinian ordered construction of many grand public works, including [[Hagia Sophia]]. The couple supported opposite sides in the Chalcedonian schism, and she is recognized as a saint in the Eastern Orthodox and Oriental Orthodox churches. Much of her life is known from the writings of Procopius, whose *Secret History* portrays her as shameless, cruel and lustful; historians are divided over its accuracy.

[[President of the United States|26th president of the United States]], serving from 1901 to 1909. A member of the [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican Party]] and the 25th vice president, he succeeded [[William McKinley]] after McKinley was assassinated and was the youngest person to become president, at 42. His "Square Deal" domestic policies called for fairness for all citizens, including breaking corporate trusts, which earned him the nickname "Trust Buster." He established national parks, forests and monuments, and he began construction of the [[Panama Canal]]. He sent the Great White Fleet on a world tour to project naval power. His efforts to end the [[Russo-Japanese War]] won him the 1906 Nobel Peace Prize, the first non-European to win a Nobel Prize. He founded the Bull Moose Party and ran in 1912, splitting the vote that allowed [[Woodrow Wilson]] to win.

King of the [[Visigoths]] from 418 to 451, who completed the Visigothic settlement in southwestern [[Gaul]] and used the declining power of the Roman Empire to extend his territory south. In 436 he sought to take Narbo Martius to gain access to the Mediterranean. In 444 the Vandal prince Huneric had Theodoric's daughter mutilated on a false accusation of plotting his death, which earned the Visigoths' enmity. Theodoric joined the Roman general [[Flavius Aetius|Aëtius]] against [[Attila]] and the [[Huns]], and his forces helped stop Attila at the Battle of the Catalaunian Plains in 451, although Theodoric was killed in the engagement.

Ostrogothic king who ruled Italy from 493 and, as regent of the [[Visigoths]] from 511, controlled an empire stretching from the [[Atlantic Ocean]] to the [[Adriatic Sea]]. Raised as a hostage in [[Constantinople]], he received an East Roman education, and in 483 the emperor Zeno made him commander of Eastern Roman forces. At Zeno's behest he attacked Odoacer in 489 and emerged victorious in 493. As king he upheld Roman legal administration and scholarly culture and promoted a major building program across Italy. He received the former Western imperial regalia from Constantinople in 497. He was buried in a grand mausoleum in [[Ravenna]], and lived on as Dietrich von Bern in Germanic heroic legend.

Roman emperor from 379 to 395, also known as Theodosius the Great. He won two civil wars and was instrumental in establishing the [[Nicene Creed]] as the orthodox doctrine, convening the First Council of Constantinople in 381. He ended the Gothic War (376–382) on terms disadvantageous to the empire, allowing the [[Goths]] to settle south of the [[Danube]] as autonomous allies. In 386 he signed a treaty with the [[Sasanian Empire]] that partitioned the long-disputed Kingdom of Armenia. He invaded the western empire to defeat the usurpers Magnus Maximus in 388 and Eugenius in 394, and he was the last emperor to rule the entire [[Roman Empire]]. After his death his sons Arcadius and Honorius ruled from separate courts in the east and west, and the division endured until the fall of the [[Western Roman Empire]] in the late 5th century.

Statement that has been proven, or can be proven, by a logical argument that applies the inference rules of a deductive system. In mainstream mathematics the axioms and inference rules are usually those of [[Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory]] with the [[Axiom of choice|axiom of choice]] (ZFC). Unlike a [[Conjecture|conjecture]], a theorem is a proved result, and many authors reserve the term for the most important results, using lemma, proposition and corollary for lesser ones. Unlike a [[Scientific law|scientific law]], whose justification is experimental, the truth of a theorem is purely deductive. [[Gödel's incompleteness theorems]] show that every consistent theory containing the natural numbers has true statements that are not theorems of the theory. Euclid proved from a few axioms that the angles of a triangle sum to 180°, but non-Euclidean geometries show that this depends on the axioms assumed.

Subfield of [[Computer science|computer science]] and mathematics that focuses on the abstract and mathematical foundations of computation. Its topics include [[Algorithm|algorithms]], [[Cryptography]], [[Information theory]], [[Computational complexity theory|computational complexity]], automata theory and quantum computation, and it is distinguished by its emphasis on mathematical technique and rigor. Its pioneers include [[Kurt Gödel]], [[Alan Turing]], [[Claude Shannon]] and Noam Chomsky. In 1931 Gödel proved that there are fundamental limits on which statements can be proved or disproved. Shannon's 1948 mathematical theory of communication added information theory to the field. In 1971 Stephen Cook and, independently, Leonid Levin proved that practically relevant problems exist that are NP-complete, a landmark result in complexity theory.

Branch of physics that uses mathematical models and abstractions of physical objects and systems to explain and predict natural phenomena. In the broadest sense it attempts to say why things happen the way they do, in contrast to experimental physics, which tests and refines those explanations. Its scope ranges from [[Elementary particle|elementary particles]] at scales far smaller than an atom to the large-scale structure of the [[Universe]]. Some of its most important results, including [[General relativity]], [[Quantum mechanics]] and the [[Standard Model]], originated as theoretical constructions before experiments confirmed them. [[Karl Popper]] argued that a scientific theory must be capable of being shown false by some possible observation. When two theories explain the same phenomena equally well, physicists generally prefer the simpler one, a principle known as [[Occam's razor]]. [[James Clerk Maxwell]] showed in the 19th century that electricity, magnetism and light are manifestations of a single electromagnetic field.
